strengths: The framework addresses a relevant autonomous-driving problem by combining dense RGB/depth supervision with safety-gated exploration. Using a shared world model for both representation learning and intrinsic rewards is a coherent design.
Table 3 provides useful evidence for dense supervision: PDMS improves from 86.2 with trajectory-only training to 87.9 with RGB, 87.8 with depth, and 88.5 with both.

Reported benchmark performance is competitive using a single front-view camera: 90.4 PDMS without best-of-six selection, 93.7 with selection, and 88.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2. The latter exceeds the strongest listed baseline by 2.7 points.
The manuscript clearly organizes the training stages, attributes its backbone and depth supervision sources, and supplies several implementation hyperparameters and qualitative results.
weaknesses: The central RL mechanism is insufficiently specified. Equation (1) defines a continuous MLP trajectory predictor, but the manuscript does not explain its stochastic policy distribution, how eight candidate trajectories are sampled, or how trajectory likelihoods and GRPO probability ratios are computed. Action conditioning of image generation and whether the reward-producing world model is frozen during RL are also unclear. These omissions prevent reproducing and assessing the main algorithm.

The uncertainty reward is both ambiguous and insufficiently validated. Equation (5) sums over token positions but omits the codebook-category sum required for categorical entropy; Equation (6) leaves the normalization function unspecified. More fundamentally, predictive entropy can reflect visual ambiguity rather than unfamiliar actions, and an OOD model can be confidently wrong. Figure 3's correlation with expert-trajectory distance and one qualitative example do not establish novelty relative to the entire training distribution.

Evidence for the principal exploration contribution is weak. In Table 4, adding the image reward to PDMS-only RL improves PDMS from 90.19 to 90.36, with no repeated-run uncertainty. Most improvement comes from task-reward RL. Comparisons against trajectory-distance novelty, policy entropy, or other intrinsic rewards, together with safety-gate and reward-weight ablations, are needed to establish the proposed mechanism's value.

The headline 93.7 PDMS depends on best-of-six selection, but the selection criterion, information available to the selector, and inference cost are not described. This makes it difficult to distinguish deployable planning performance from an oracle selection result. Table 2 also leaves its sampling/selection protocol unclear, and no uncertainty is reported for the small 0.2-point lead over DriveSuprim in Table 1.

Claims of discovering robust OOD strategies exceed the evaluation. There is no explicit distribution-shift or behavioral-coverage experiment, and NAVSIM's non-reactive evaluation does not establish safety under interactive closed-loop deployment. The nuScenes experiment uses only Stage 1, so it does not validate transfer of the exploration mechanism. Furthermore, the world model predicts only 0.5 seconds ahead while NAVSIM trajectories span four seconds, leaving the reward's sensitivity to later behavioral differences unexamined.

Originality beyond existing unified world-model/planning approaches rests primarily on the entropy reward, whose benefit remains uncertain. The dense-supervision component is better supported, but the supplied evidence does not yet compensate for the methodological and validation gaps in the paper's main claimed contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant autonomous-driving problem by combining dense future RGB/depth supervision with an uncertainty-based exploration reward. The distinction between trajectory quality and novelty is useful, and conditioning the exploration bonus on a high PDMS is a reasonable practical design.

The dense-supervision contribution has concrete empirical support. In Table 3, RGB and depth individually improve PDMS from 86.2 to 87.9 and 87.8, respectively, while their combination reaches 88.5. These controlled comparisons support complementary benefits from appearance and geometry supervision.

Reported NAVSIM performance is competitive with a single front-view camera: 90.4 PDMS without best-of-six selection, 93.7 with selection, and 88.8 EPDMS on v2. The supplementary nuScenes results provide additional evidence for the Stage 1 model, including a competitive average collision rate.

The manuscript is generally readable, acknowledges closely related unified planning/generation approaches, and attributes its backbone, tokenizer, and depth-label source. The supplement provides useful training hyperparameters and qualitative predictions.
weaknesses: The central exploration contribution has limited empirical support. Table 4 shows that PDMS-only RL improves the Stage 1 baseline from 88.50 to 90.19, while adding the proposed image reward reaches 90.36: an incremental gain of only 0.17 points without multiple seeds or uncertainty estimates. There is no corresponding reward ablation on NAVSIM v2 or under best-of-six selection. Figure 4 compares Stage 1 against full RL, so its improvements cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed exploration mechanism.

The interpretation of token entropy as distance from the expert trajectory distribution is not established. Predictive entropy can reflect visual ambiguity, texture complexity, or model error rather than behavioral novelty. Figure 3 provides a correlation with trajectory L2 distance and one illustrative counterexample, but no independently defined novelty measure, OOD evaluation, or comparison against simpler novelty bonuses. The claim that the reward identifies genuinely new successful strategies therefore exceeds the evidence.

Essential details of the RL algorithm are missing. Equation (1) specifies a continuous MLP waypoint predictor, but the manuscript does not define the stochastic trajectory distribution, sampling procedure, or trajectory log-likelihood needed for GRPO probability ratios and KL regularization. Action conditioning is described verbally but omitted from the image-generation equations, and the action-supervision loss is unspecified. Appendix A's hyperparameters do not resolve these implementation gaps.

The intrinsic reward itself is insufficiently specified. As written, Equation (5) sums over image positions using each selected token's probability, rather than summing over the codebook distribution at every position; this is not the stated categorical entropy. The normalization function in Equation (6) is also undefined. Additionally, it is unclear whether the world model is frozen during RL despite sharing the policy backbone. These details determine the reward's meaning, scale, and stability, so they are more consequential than cosmetic notation issues.

The headline evaluation needs clearer inference protocols. The 93.7 PDMS result depends on best-of-six selection, but the manuscript does not explain the selection criterion or information available to the selector. Table 2 does not clarify whether the same procedure is used. Inference latency and generation/selection overhead are unreported, limiting assessment of the practical value and comparability of the reported gains.

Broader generalization and safety claims are not adequately tested. NAVSIM uses non-reactive evaluation, and nuScenes evaluates only Stage 1, explicitly excluding the proposed RL mechanism. Consequently, neither establishes improved exploration under distribution shift or safety in reactive interactions. Assessed as an Algorithms/General submission, the work has promising supervised-learning results, but unresolved algorithmic details and weak isolation of its principal novelty favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: combining dense visual supervision with policy exploration for autonomous driving. Using an action-conditioned world model both for representation learning and for an intrinsic reward is a coherent and potentially useful direction.
Reported NAVSIM performance is strong with only front-view camera inputs: 93.7 PDMS with best-of-six selection and 88.8 EPDMS. The latter exceeds the strongest comparator in Table 2 by 2.7 points.

Table 3 provides useful evidence for dense supervision. RGB generation improves PDMS from 86.2 to 87.9, depth generation achieves 87.8, and their combination reaches 88.5, supporting complementary benefits.

The manuscript is generally well organized, acknowledges closely related unified planning and generation methods, and supplies supplementary implementation settings and qualitative predictions. The additional nuScenes evaluation provides evidence for the Stage 1 model, including a competitive average ST-P3 collision rate.
weaknesses: The central RL mechanism is insufficiently specified to establish technical soundness or reproducibility. Equation (1) defines a continuous MLP trajectory output, but the paper does not explain the stochastic policy distribution, how eight candidate trajectories are sampled, or how their likelihoods and GRPO likelihood ratios are computed. Appendix A supplies clipping and KL coefficients without resolving this interface. The trajectory-conditioning implementation and whether the reward-producing world model is frozen during RL are also unclear; updating that model could change the reward independently of behavioral novelty.

The interpretation of image-token entropy as distance from the entire expert distribution is not established. Predictive entropy can reflect ambiguous scene dynamics, visual complexity, or model error, and an out-of-distribution input need not produce high entropy. Figure 3 offers a scatter plot and one illustrative comparison, without a quantitative evaluation of novelty detection or separation of these confounders. Moreover, Equation (5), as written, sums probabilities of individual image tokens over positions rather than summing over the codebook at each position, so it does not define the stated categorical entropy. The normalization function in Equation (6) is unspecified.

The evidence for the distinctive exploration contribution is weak relative to the claims. In Table 4, PDMS-only RL improves 88.50 to 90.19, while adding the proposed exploration reward yields only 90.36. Without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, the reliability of this 0.17-point increment is unclear. There are no comparisons against simpler novelty bonuses, controlled distribution-shift experiments, or quantitative behavioral-diversity measurements. Figure 4 compares imitation learning against the complete RL system and therefore cannot isolate the exploration bonus.

The headline results need a clearer evaluation protocol. The 93.7 PDMS result relies on best-of-six selection, but the scoring and selection procedure, required information, and computational cost are not specified. Table 2 does not clarify whether the same selection is used. Without selection, the NAVSIM v1 improvement over DriveVLA-W0 is only 90.4 versus 90.2. The absence of exploration ablations on NAVSIM v2 also leaves the larger EPDMS gain unattributed.

Claims about OOD generalization and safe exploration exceed the demonstrated scope. NAVSIM provides non-reactive evaluation, and thresholding its aggregate score is not a general safety guarantee. Appendix B.2 explicitly evaluates only Stage 1 on nuScenes, so those results do not validate the proposed RL exploration mechanism across datasets. Given that dense world-model supervision already has substantial precedent, the unresolved specification and limited validation of the exploration mechanism leave important concerns for acceptance under Algorithms/General.
